candidates.title: Secret-bearing temp file is briefly left at umask permissions (0644) before chmod to 0600
candidates.source: Rotated OAuth tokens (refresh_token/access_token/id_token) serialized by FileCredentialReader.writeBack (Sources/AiTaskbarCore/Credentials/FileCredentialReader.swift:74), and other 0o600 callers (config.toml with inline api_key)
candidates.sink: Sources/AiTaskbarCore/Cache/AtomicFileWrite.swift:19 creates the temp file with the default mode (0666 & ~umask, so 0644). The 0o600 chmod only happens afterwards, at line 21-24.
candidates.description: The temp file is fully created and populated with the secret payload by `Data.write(.atomic)`, which gives new files the default mode. `setAttributes(0o600)` runs only after that. For that interval the plaintext tokens sit world-readable in the destination directory. The doc comment claims this race is avoided, but it has only moved from the final path to the temp path. That breaks the hard rule of '0o600 at write time'. For ~/.codex, which the app does not force to 0700 (only its own Application Support and Caches dirs get 0700), the directory is typically traversable by other local users.
candidates.exploit_scenario: On a multi-user Mac, another local user watches ~/.codex with kqueue/FSEvents for `.auth.json.*.tmp` and calls open() the moment the file appears. An fd opened while the mode is 0644 keeps its read access after the chmod and rename. The attacker then reads the rotated Codex refresh_token and can take over the victim's ChatGPT/Codex session.
preconditions: another local OS user on the same Mac
~/.codex (or the destination dir) is traversable by others (not 0700)
manage_oauth_refresh = true for the Codex write-back path (off by default); config.toml writes land in the 0700 app-support dir, so they are not reachable
candidates.impact: Disclosure of a rotated OAuth refresh token (Codex) to another local user
candidates.fix: Create the temp file with the final mode from the start: open(tmp, O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_WRONLY|O_NOFOLLOW, 0o600) (or mkstemp + fchmod before any write), write, fsync, then rename(2). Do not use Data.write(.atomic) for this.
candidates.evidence: AtomicFileWrite.swift:19 `try data.write(to: tmp, options: .atomic)` then :20-24 `if let permissions { try FileManager.default.setAttributes([.posixPermissions: ...], ofItemAtPath: tmp.path) }`. FileCredentialReader.swift:74 passes permissions: 0o600 for ~/.codex/auth.json. Paths.swift:86-102 ensureDir does not tighten the mode of ~/.codex.

candidates.title: Fallback metadata query runs outside prompt suppression and without UIFail, including on the locked-keychain path
candidates.snippet: guard SecItemCopyMatching(query as CFDictionary, &result) == errSecSuccess, let ref = result else {
candidates.source: A scheduled refresh reaches readData (KeychainCredentialReader.swift:156-166). The suppressed direct read fast-fails with -25308/-25293. That also happens when the item's keychain has been locked since the target was bound (resolvedTarget skips the suppressed candidateMatches search once target is set).
candidates.sink: KeychainCredentialReader.swift:218. An unsuppressed SecItemCopyMatching (kSecMatchItemList + kSecReturnRef) runs with no kSecUseAuthenticationUI key, called from readViaSecurityTool at line 187.
candidates.description: Every other Keychain call in the component is wrapped in KeychainPromptSuppressor.withPromptsSuppressed and passes kSecUseAuthenticationUIFail. itemKeychain does neither, and the suppressor's resting state is interaction ALLOWED (exit() applies true at depth 0). This query runs specifically after an ACL/locked fast-fail, which is exactly when the item's keychain may be locked. On classic file keychains, looking up an item in a locked keychain while interaction is allowed can raise the SecurityAgent unlock dialog. That breaks the hard rule that scheduled reads never prompt, and the isUnlocked guard runs only after this call.
candidates.exploit_scenario: 1) The app binds the Claude credential target while the login keychain is unlocked. 2) The login keychain auto-locks (sleep or lock timeout). 3) The next 300 s scheduled refresh does a suppressed read, which fast-fails, and then calls itemKeychain with prompts enabled. 4) securityd may show an 'unlock keychain' password dialog on behalf of an LSUIElement app with no visible window. The refresh stalls, and the user learns to type their login password into unexplained prompts.
preconditions: Direct read already fast-fails (ad-hoc/unauthorized build or locked keychain)
Target identity already bound from an earlier successful search
securityd raises unlock UI for a ref lookup in a locked file keychain (not verified here)
candidates.impact: An unrequested Keychain password or unlock prompt can appear outside the Authorize flow, and the refresh cycle can freeze behind it. This is defense in depth. No credential is disclosed.
candidates.fix: Run the itemKeychain query inside KeychainPromptSuppressor.withPromptsSuppressed and add kSecUseAuthenticationUI: kSecUseAuthenticationUIFail, the same as exactQuery and candidateMatches. Or take the SecKeychainItem ref from the already-suppressed candidateMatches result and cache it with the TargetIdentity, so no new lookup is needed on the fallback path.
candidates.evidence: KeychainCredentialReader.swift:211-218: the query dict has no kSecUseAuthenticationUI and the call is not wrapped. KeychainPromptSuppressor.swift:111-119: the depth-0 state applies setInteractionAllowed(true). KeychainCredentialReader.swift:187: itemKeychain runs before Self.isUnlocked(keychain). Compare KeychainAccessAuthorizer.swift:234-239 (candidateMatches, suppressed + UIFail) and KeychainCredentialReader.swift:254-266 (exactQuery, suppressed + UIFail).

candidates.title: Built-in TLS pins for vendor hosts are never enforced unless the host is also listed in pin_hosts, which is empty by default
candidates.source: Any TLS server presenting a certificate for api.anthropic.com, chatgpt.com, auth.openai.com, openrouter.ai, management-api.x.ai and similar hosts. Pinning turns on only when cfg.security.pinHosts is non-empty (AppEnvironment.swift:30). pinHosts defaults to [] (AppConfig.swift:106/119), and the shipped config.toml leaves the line commented out (ConfigLoader.swift:312).
candidates.sink: PinningDelegate.swift:36-44 passes any host missing from pinnedHosts to .performDefaultHandling (system trust only). PinBaseline.pin(for:) is only reached at line 63, after that guard. On top of that, HTTPClient.pinned returns an unpinned HTTPClient() when pinnedHosts is empty (HTTPClient.swift:39-40).
candidates.description: PinBaseline's own comment says it closes the first-connection window for every vendor host. The settings UI tells users 'Baseline pins for known vendor hosts ship in-binary — leave empty unless you have a private endpoint.' In the code, though, a baseline pin is only checked for hosts that are already in the user-supplied pinnedHosts set, and with the default empty list no delegate is installed at all. OAuth bearer tokens and API keys are therefore protected only by system trust, while the product says pinning is on.
candidates.exploit_scenario: 1) The attacker gets a root CA trusted on the victim's Mac: a corporate TLS-inspection proxy, malware-installed root, MDM profile, or a CA mis-issuance for a vendor domain. 2) The victim runs ai-taskbar with the default config and follows the UI advice to leave pin_hosts empty. 3) The attacker intercepts the refresh to api.anthropic.com or chatgpt.com. System trust accepts the forged leaf and no SPKI check runs. 4) The attacker captures the Authorization: Bearer OAuth access token (and, when manage_oauth_refresh=true, the refresh token sent to platform.claude.com or auth.openai.com), which gives access to the user's Claude/ChatGPT account.
preconditions: Attacker-controlled certificate that the victim's system trusts (rogue or corporate root CA, or mis-issuance)
Default config (pin_hosts empty), which the settings UI recommends
candidates.impact: Theft of vendor OAuth/API credentials by an on-path attacker that the shipped baseline pins were meant to stop. This is a defense-in-depth failure made worse because users are told the protection is active.
candidates.fix: Always install PinningDelegate, and make the effective pin set Set(PinBaseline.baselineHosts.keys) ∪ pin_hosts. HTTPClient.pinned should return a pinned session even when pin_hosts is empty, and the host check should be pinnedHosts.contains(host) || PinBaseline.pin(for: host) != nil. If the current behavior is intentional, correct the UI strings and the PinBaseline doc comment instead.
candidates.evidence: AppEnvironment.swift:30-37: `if !cfg.security.pinHosts.isEmpty { http = try HTTPClient.pinned(...) } else { http = HTTPClient() }`. HTTPClient.swift:39-40: `guard !pinnedHosts.isEmpty else { return HTTPClient() }`. PinningDelegate.swift:36: the membership check runs before PinBaseline.pin(for:) at line 63. en.lproj/Localizable.strings:153/210 claim baseline pins ship in the binary and advise leaving the field empty.

candidates.title: Session JSONL files are memory-mapped, so truncating one mid-scan raises SIGBUS
candidates.snippet: guard let data = try? Data(contentsOf: url, options: [.mappedIfSafe]) else { continue }
candidates.sink: Mapped Data read byte by byte in scan(data:), via firstIndex(of:) and range(of:) at ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:203-211; the same pattern is at CodexSessionScanner.swift:128 and 322-329
candidates.description: On a local volume, .mappedIfSafe mmaps the file. If the file shrinks after mapping, touching a page past the new end of file raises SIGBUS, which Swift cannot catch. No snapshot, file lock or read-copy guard covers the mapped bytes while the line scanner walks them.
candidates.exploit_scenario: A same-user process creates a large *.jsonl with a recent mtime in ~/.claude/projects/x/ and truncates and rewrites it in a tight loop. When a refresh maps the file and the scanner touches a page past the truncated end, the process dies with SIGBUS. Refreshes run every 300 s and on every launch, so the crash repeats.
preconditions: Write access to ~/.claude/projects or ~/.codex/sessions
Winning a race between the mmap and the scan, which is easy to repeat because every refresh re-maps changed files
candidates.impact: Repeatable crash of the menu-bar app (denial of service). Nothing is disclosed.
candidates.fix: Read with a regular read (no .mappedIfSafe, or .uncached), or read from an open FileHandle into an owned buffer so a concurrent truncation can only produce a short read.
candidates.evidence: ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:91 and CodexSessionScanner.swift:128 both use [.mappedIfSafe]; the scan loops then iterate the whole mapped Data.

candidates.title: A crafted opencode message crashes the app: the output + reasoning addition does not saturate
candidates.source: The JSON `data` column of the `message` table in ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db: $.tokens.output and $.tokens.reasoning (OpencodeScanner.swift:141-142)
candidates.sink: Swift's checked `+` on two Int values, each clamped only from below (OpencodeScanner.swift:197)
candidates.description: The scanner reads two per-group sums from SQLite: sum($.tokens.output) and sum($.tokens.reasoning). Each is clamped with max(0, x), which puts no upper bound on either value, and then the two are added with Swift's `+`, which traps on overflow. Only this addition skips CostAggregator.saturatingAdd. The CodexSessionScanner and ClaudeSessionScanner paths use it or clamp their subtractions.
candidates.exploit_scenario: Write one assistant row into opencode.db with providerID set to a tracked alias (such as openai), a recent time_created, and tokens.output = 9223372036854775807 plus tokens.reasoning = 1. A REAL such as 1e300 also works, because sqlite3_column_int64 clamps it to Int64.max. SQLite's sum() does not overflow on a single row. On the next refresh the Swift addition hits SIGTRAP and the menu-bar app exits. The row stays in the database, so every relaunch and refresh crashes again until the row is removed.
preconditions: Write access to ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db (another tool or a prompt-injected agent running as the same user)
opencode cost scanning is enabled for at least one vendor
candidates.impact: Persistent denial of service: the app crashes on every refresh cycle, so all usage monitoring stops.
candidates.fix: Use CostAggregator.saturatingAdd(max(0, output), max(0, reasoning)). Better still, clamp each column to a sane per-group ceiling before any arithmetic.
candidates.evidence: L187 `let reasoning = Int(sqlite3_column_int64(stmt, 5))`; L197 uses a bare `+`. By contrast CostAggregator.add (CostAggregator.swift:16-30) and ClaudeSessionScanner L232 use saturatingAdd.

candidates.title: Huge utilization value in Anthropic usage JSON crashes the app on every launch
candidates.source: Response body of GET https://api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage: five_hour/seven_day/seven_day_opus.utilization, limits[].percent, extra_usage.utilization (AnthropicWireTypes.swift:42,71,100)
candidates.description: The Anthropic decoder accepts any finite Double, e.g. 1e300, as a utilization percent. toSnapshot (AnthropicWireTypes.swift:145-149, 168-173, 185) and UsageWindow.init copy it without a range or finiteness clamp. VendorSnapshot.maxUtilization (UsageSnapshot.swift:71) and UsageStore aggregate compute (UsageStore.swift:379) then pass it to the menu-bar label, whose Int(Double) conversion traps when the value does not fit in Int.
candidates.exploit_scenario: The usage endpoint returns {"five_hour":{"utilization":1e300}}. Decoding succeeds, CachedFetch writes the payload to the disk cache (CachedFetch.swift:34-36), and the menu-bar label renders Int(1e300.rounded()), which is a fatal trap. On relaunch the cached payload decodes the same way and crashes again until the cache expires or is removed. Stale fallback keeps serving it if the next fetch fails.
preconditions: Attacker controls the Anthropic usage API response (malicious or compromised vendor; TLS rules out an ordinary MITM)
Anthropic card is expanded (default) or a notification threshold fires
candidates.impact: Denial of service of the local menu-bar app (repeated crash loop through the disk cache); stops monitoring of every vendor. No data exposure.
candidates.fix: Sanitize at the wire-to-snapshot boundary. In toSnapshot, or centrally in UsageWindow.init, drop non-finite values and clamp to a sane range (e.g. 0...1000) before building UsageWindow. Optionally, in the UI use Int(exactly:) or a checked conversion instead of Int(Double).
candidates.evidence: AppConfig.swift:199-203 flexibleDoubleIfPresent returns any decoded Double; UsageWindow.swift:15-23 stores it as-is; UsageSnapshot.swift:70-72 max(); MenuBarLabelView.swift:39-41 Int(percent.rounded()); NotificationService.swift:102 Int(window.utilizationPercent).

candidates.title: Antigravity remaining_fraction out of range crashes the app in Int(Double)
candidates.source: `agy /usage` JSON output (GeminiProvider.swift:71) and the generativelanguage.googleapis.com /models body (GeminiProvider.swift:94). decodeSnapshot tries both as AntigravityUsageResponse (GeminiProvider.swift:101)
candidates.description: `remaining_fraction` is decoded as an unbounded Double. The clamp at line 151 only covers consumedFraction. The raw `rem` is multiplied by 100 and passed to Int(), which traps when the value is beyond Int range (for example 1e300 or -1e300). decodeSnapshot tries AntigravityUsageResponse first on every payload, so any response with `command.name == "usage"` reaches this line, whether it comes from agy or from the HTTP heartbeat.
candidates.exploit_scenario: A hostile or compromised upstream returns {"command":{"name":"usage","data":{"groups":[{"name":"gemini","buckets":[{"window":"5h","remaining_fraction":1e300}]}]}}}. CachedFetch writes the payload to the DiskCache, and decoding it traps the process. Later launches that decode the cached payload inside the TTL crash again.
preconditions: attacker controls the agy output or the Gemini API response body
Gemini provider enabled
candidates.impact: Local DoS: the menu-bar app crashes and can keep crashing on relaunch while the cached payload is still valid.
candidates.fix: Clamp or reject non-finite and out-of-range values before converting: let r = rem.isFinite ? min(max(rem, 0), 1) : 1. Then use Int((r*100).rounded()), or validate remaining_fraction to 0...1 in the decoder.
candidates.evidence: L150 `let rem = bucket.remainingFraction ?? 1.0`. L151 clamps only consumedFraction. L154 converts the unclamped `rem` with Int(). GeminiProvider.swift:101 always tries this decoder first.

candidates.title: Unbounded Grok creditUsagePercent reaches Int() in the menu-bar label and crashes the app
candidates.source: cli-chat-proxy.grok.com /v1/billing response, field config.creditUsagePercent (XAIProvider.swift:89-92, default preferGrokCLI=true)
candidates.description: creditUsagePercent is decoded as an unbounded Double and copied unchanged into UsageWindow.utilizationPercent. Neither UsageWindow.init nor UsageSnapshot.maxUtilization nor AggregatesComputation clamps it. The UI then calls Int(percent.rounded()), which traps for values beyond Int range.
candidates.exploit_scenario: The billing endpoint returns {"config":{"creditUsagePercent":1e300}}. The value becomes the weekly window and maxUtilization. The menu-bar label evaluates Int(1e300.rounded()) and the process traps. The cached payload keeps the crash going on relaunch.
preconditions: attacker controls the Grok CLI proxy response body
xAI provider enabled with ~/.grok/auth.json present
candidates.impact: Local DoS of the whole menu-bar app, not only the xAI card.
candidates.fix: Clamp or validate percentages at the wire boundary: guard isFinite, then clamp to 0...some max. Also make UsageWindow.init sanitize utilizationPercent so every vendor is covered.
candidates.evidence: XAIWireTypes.swift:266 `let util = cfg.creditUsagePercent ?? 0.0`, passed as utilizationPercent: util at L270. UsageWindow.swift:20 stores it with no clamp. MenuBarLabelView.swift:41 `Int(percent.rounded())`.

candidates.title: Huge limit_window_seconds in the vendor response crashes the app on Int(Double) conversion
candidates.source: Response body of GET https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/wham/usage, field rate_limit.primary_window/secondary_window.limit_window_seconds, decoded at OpenAIWireTypes.swift:76 by flexibleDoubleIfPresent
candidates.sink: OpenAIWireTypes.swift:211 (and :213 for the hours branch): Int(days.rounded())
candidates.description: limit_window_seconds is decoded into a Double with no range check. humanLabel only checks s > 0. A finite but huge JSON number like 1e300 passes both, days becomes about 1e295, and Int(_:) on an out-of-range Double traps. The process aborts inside decodeSnapshot.
candidates.exploit_scenario: The vendor endpoint, or anything that controls the response, returns {"rate_limit":{"primary_window":{"used_percent":1,"limit_window_seconds":1e300}}}. On every refresh, OpenAIProvider.decodeSnapshot calls toSnapshot, then window(), then kind.label(from:), and the menu-bar app crashes. CachedFetch decodes before it writes the cache (CachedFetch.swift:34-36), so the bad payload is not saved and the crash does not survive a relaunch by itself. It repeats as long as the server keeps sending the value.
preconditions: attacker controls the chatgpt.com usage response (hostile or compromised vendor); TLS rules out a network MITM
candidates.impact: The local monitor app is knocked out (crashes) for as long as the payload is served. No data exposure.
candidates.fix: Reject non-finite or absurd values before converting, e.g. guard let s = seconds, s.isFinite, s > 0, s < 10 * 365 * 86_400 else { return default }. Or use Int(exactly:) / a clamped conversion so no trap is possible.
candidates.evidence: OpenAIWireTypes.swift:207 `guard let s = seconds, s > 0` (no upper bound or isFinite check), :211/:213 `Int(days.rounded())` / `Int(hours.rounded())`. SharedCoders.decoder sets no nonConformingFloatDecodingStrategy, so only finite values arrive, but 1e300 is finite and is well past Int.max days.

candidates.title: Z.AI quota response with an out-of-range unit/number crashes the app (Int(Double) trap), and the crash repeats from the disk cache
candidates.source: Response body of GET https://api.z.ai/api/monitor/usage/quota/limit (ZAIProvider.swift:50, http.fetchPayload), decoded in ZAIProvider.decodeSnapshot (ZAIProvider.swift:58)
candidates.sink: Sources/AiTaskbarProviders/ZAIWireTypes.swift:83 and :84, where Int($0) converts a Double that was never checked for range
candidates.description: flexibleDoubleIfPresent (AppConfig.swift:199-203) accepts any finite JSON number as a Double, and the code passes it straight to Int(_:) with no range or isFinite check. In Swift, Int(Double) is a runtime trap when the value does not fit in Int (above about 9.22e18), so this is a crash rather than a thrown error. The decode happens in decodeSnapshot, which is not protected by the do/catch around it, because a trap cannot be caught.
candidates.exploit_scenario: The Z.AI endpoint, or anything that can shape its JSON, returns {"code":200,"success":true,"data":{"limits":[{"type":"TOKENS_LIMIT","unit":1e19,"number":1}]}}. ZAILimitEntry.init calls Int(1e19) and the process aborts. CachedFetch saves the raw payload in the DiskCache, so every later cache or stale-fallback decode aborts again, until the cache is cleared or overwritten by a clean fetch.
preconditions: Z.AI provider enabled
attacker controls or influences the Z.AI API response (the threat model given)
candidates.impact: Denial of service for the menu-bar app (crash, possibly a crash loop while the poisoned cache entry lasts). No confidentiality or integrity impact.
candidates.fix: Convert with Int(exactly:) after rounding, or check range first, and return nil when the value is out of range, for example flexibleDoubleIfPresent(...).flatMap { $0.isFinite ? Int(exactly: $0.rounded()) : nil }. Consider a shared flexibleIntIfPresent helper in Core that decodes Int64 first and uses an exact conversion as the fallback.
candidates.evidence: ZAIWireTypes.swift:83-84 `.map { Int($0) }` on the result of flexibleDoubleIfPresent, and AppConfig.swift:200 `try? decodeIfPresent(Double.self…)` accepts values like 1e19. There is no other place where unit or number are checked before this conversion.

candidates.title: Update DMG accepted with no integrity anchor outside the release and no quarantine flag, so Gatekeeper never checks it
candidates.source: GitHub Releases API response (tag_name, assets[].browser_download_url, assets[].size, checksums-*.txt asset), Sources/AiTaskbarApp/UpdateChecker.swift:165-196
candidates.sink: DMG promoted into ~/Downloads and shown in Finder for the user to install, Sources/AiTaskbarApp/UpdateChecker.swift:265 and :275
candidates.description: Every integrity input comes from the same release the attacker controls. The size comes from the asset metadata. The SHA-256 comes from a sibling checksums-*.txt asset in that release, and a missing or unparseable checksums file (`try?` at :186) turns the check off entirely (fail-open, :259). Nothing checks the DMG, or the app inside it, against the app's own Developer ID team (CodeSignatureInfo.currentTeamID exists but is never used here). The comment at :267-274 says Gatekeeper is the last line of defence. But the file is fetched with URLSession.download in an app that is not sandboxed (entitlements.plist app-sandbox=false), and Info.plist has no LSFileQuarantineEnabled. So the file gets no com.apple.quarantine flag, and Gatekeeper never assesses the DMG or the .app copied out of it.
candidates.exploit_scenario: 1) The attacker gets write access to the release repo (stolen maintainer token or compromised account) and publishes v99.0.0. The release holds an unsigned or ad-hoc-signed ai-taskbar-99.0.0-arm64.dmg and optionally a matching checksums-99.0.0.txt, or no checksums file at all. 2) Within 24 h every installed copy sees Semver.isNewer('v99.0.0', current) == true and shows the update banner. 3) The user clicks Download. The size and hash match because the attacker wrote both, the file is moved to ~/Downloads without quarantine, and Finder reveals it. 4) The user mounts it and drags the app to /Applications, as the app tells them to. On launch there is no Gatekeeper or notarization prompt, because the file has no quarantine flag. The attacker's code runs as the user and can read the Claude/Codex OAuth tokens and API keys this app handles.
preconditions: attacker can publish a release on the configured updates owner/repo (compromised maintainer account or token)
user clicks Download and installs the DMG as instructed
candidates.impact: Arbitrary code runs as the user on every installed copy that accepts the update. That exposes the Keychain-held Claude credentials, ~/.codex/auth.json, and vendor API keys.
candidates.fix: Before moving or revealing the DMG, verify it against an anchor that is not in the release. Mount it read-only (hdiutil attach -nobrowse -readonly), then run SecStaticCodeCheckValidity on the bundled .app with a requirement that pins anchor apple generic plus certificate leaf[subject.OU] = the running app's team ID (CodeSignatureInfo.currentTeamID). Also require a notarization ticket (stapler/spctl assessment). Fail closed when the running build has no team ID, instead of skipping. Set com.apple.quarantine on the downloaded file (or add LSFileQuarantineEnabled) so Gatekeeper still runs. Treat a missing checksum as an error, not as a skip.
candidates.evidence: :179-187 the checksum comes from an asset in the same release, fetched with try? (fail-open). :252-264 size/hash come from the release, and the hash is optional. :265 moveItem and :275 activateFileViewerSelecting run with no codesign or team check. HTTPClient.download (Sources/AiTaskbarCore/Networking/HTTPClient.swift:71) is a plain session.download, and nothing sets xattr quarantine. Resources/entitlements.plist sets app-sandbox false, and Resources/Info.plist has no LSFileQuarantineEnabled. CodeSignatureInfo is only used by the Keychain code and AboutView, never by UpdateChecker.

candidates.title: AtomicFileWrite overwrite of an existing file keeps its old (looser) mode: replaceItemAt preserves original metadata, so write(permissions:0o600) leaves a 0644 secret file at 0644
candidates.source: any existing secret file (config.toml with inline api_key, ~/.codex/auth.json write-back) that is 0644 before the write
candidates.description: `_ = try FileManager.default.replaceItemAt(dest, withItemAt: tmp)`. By default replaceItemAt keeps the original item's metadata, permissions included. Checked with a scratch Swift probe: dest chmod 0644, tmp chmod 0600, after replaceItemAt the mode printed `644`. Every permission test writes a NEW file: AiTaskbarValidate/main.swift:798, UsageHistoryStoreTests.swift:27-33, ConfigLoaderSecretTests.swift:212-225.
candidates.exploit_scenario: A credential file exists at 0644 (created by another tool, restored from backup, or user chmod). The app rewrites it with permissions 0o600 expecting to tighten it; replaceItemAt keeps 0644; other local users can read the secret.
preconditions: secret file pre-exists with loose mode
multi-user Mac or other-uid process
candidates.impact: Once a secret file exists with a loose mode, every later write(permissions:0o600) leaves it 0644. That breaks the 0o600-at-write-time rule, and the suite stays green.
candidates.fix: Add a test that pre-creates dest at 0644. Use .usingNewMetadataOnly, rename(2), or an explicit final mode.
candidates.evidence: `_ = try FileManager.default.replaceItemAt(dest, withItemAt: tmp)`. By default replaceItemAt keeps the original item's metadata, permissions included. Checked with a scratch Swift probe: dest chmod 0644, tmp chmod 0600, after replaceItemAt the mode printed `644`. Every permission test writes a NEW file: AiTaskbarValidate/main.swift:798, UsageHistoryStoreTests.swift:27-33, ConfigLoaderSecretTests.swift:212-225.
candidates.origin: Argus (tests lens) — security-relevant, sent to panel

candidates.title: Crash persists after the vendor recovers: an oversized utilization is saved to 90-day history and replayed into Int() on the analytics busiest-day label
candidates.source: Any vendor utilization field, e.g. Sources/AiTaskbarProviders/AnthropicWireTypes.swift:71 or ZAIWireTypes.swift:88, then VendorViewModel.recordHistory (Sources/AiTaskbarApp/ViewModels/VendorViewModel.swift:235,276)
candidates.description: One response with a finite value of at least 9.3e18 (for example 1e300) sets snapshot.maxUtilization. recordHistory appends it to <vendor>.jsonl before SwiftUI renders anything, so the value is on disk even if the menu bar then crashes. compact() keeps samples for 90 days. AnalyticsStore loads 90 days of history (AnalyticsStore.swift:203). computePeakDay (AnalyticsAggregator.swift:29-47) picks that sample as the busiest day, and peakDayText converts it with Int() without a check. AnalyticsAggregator.swift:124-125 also feeds historyMax into totalUsagePercent when there is no live snapshot, and that reaches Int() at VendorAnalyticsCardView.swift:102.
candidates.exploit_scenario: 1) The vendor endpoint, or a MITM holding a trusted certificate, returns utilization 1e300 once. 2) The app appends {"max":1e300} to history. 3) The vendor goes back to normal values, so the menu bar and cache are fine again. 4) For the next 90 days, opening the Analytics dashboard computes the peak day and aborts the process, every time and after every relaunch.
preconditions: The attacker controls one usage response from any enabled vendor (malicious or compromised vendor, or a TLS MITM)
The user opens the Analytics view within 90 days
candidates.impact: A lasting crash of the analytics feature that survives relaunch and outlives the attack. Recovery needs manual deletion of the history JSONL.
candidates.fix: Clamp and finite-check utilization when UsageWindow is built (for example min(max(x,0),1000)), also clamp in UsageHistoryStore.append/load, and use a non-trapping formatter such as Int(exactly:) or clamp before Int() in the views.
candidates.evidence: VendorViewModel.swift:229-235 sets state and appends history synchronously. UsageHistoryStore.swift:56-67 does no validation. UsageHistoryStore.defaultRetention is 90*86_400. AnalyticsAggregator.swift:29 is dayMaxes max(). AnalyticsFormatters.swift:46,48 call Int().
